transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
I came in because I can’t shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. Ever since the divorce, it feels like everything I built has collapsed, and I’m just sitting under it.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, hopeless way?
About a month now. It really started after the financial mess from the divorce hit.
Have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy doing?
I’m not really sure. I just know everything feels heavy right now.
How has your sleep been over the past month?
It’s been pretty bad. Some nights I just lie awake staring at the ceiling, going over bills and mistakes at work. Other times I wake up before dawn and feel like I barely slept at all.
Have you ever had a period in your life where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or hyper, where you felt like you didn't need much sleep?
Yes. There were several nights when I only slept maybe two or three hours, but I still felt sharp enough to keep working. Sleep just seemed like an inefficient use of time then.
About how long did that period of high energy and needing very little sleep last?
About two weeks, I think. I was intensely wired at first, and then it started turning into a crash.
During that two-week period when you felt so wired, did it cause serious problems in your work or personal life?

Yes. I was making questionable calls at work and falling apart in meetings. My supervisor had to take me off active project decisions. At home, I stopped keeping up with basic routines, and it got bad enough that I was sent to the emergency department because I didn’t feel safe with my thoughts.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a current depressive episode lasting one month, characterized by persistent low mood, feelings of hopelessness, and insomnia. Assessment of past psychiatric history revealed a distinct two-week episode of mania marked by abnormally elevated energy, decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours per night without fatigue), and marked impairment in occupational and social functioning leading to removal from work duties and an emergency department evaluation. The occurrence of at least one manic episode alongside depressive episodes meets the criteria for bipolar affective disorder (F31).
